title: Session 14: Case 2-1 and Case 3-1, Maynard Company (A) and (B)

slides.visual_text: A scanned textbook page: Chapter 2, Basic Accounting Concepts: The Balance Sheet, Cases, Case 2-1, Maynard Company (A), credited to Professor Robert N. Anthony. Story in brief: Diane Maynard's bookkeeper has quit and she asks a friend to prepare her company's balance sheets from the book he left, and to comment on the numbers. She says the Cash account is healthy and that the bookkeeper told her net income in June was $19,635. The friend copies the account balances at the beginning and end of the month (Exhibit 1). Diane Maynard owned all the stock of Maynard Company; at the end of June she paid herself an $11,700 dividend and used it to repay her loan from the company. Questions: 1. Prepare balance sheets as of June 1 and June 30, in proper format. 2. Comment on how the financial condition at the end of June compared with the beginning of June. 3. Why do retained earnings not increase by the amount of June net income? 4. As of June 30, is Maynard Company worth the amount in Shareholder's Equity, $619,446? Explain. Exhibit 1, Account Balances (June 1; June 30): Accounts payable $8,517; $21,315. Accounts receivable 21,798; 26,505. Accrued wages payable 1,974; 2,202. Accumulated depreciation on building 156,000; 157,950. Accumulated depreciation on equipment 5,304; 5,928. Bank notes payable 8,385; 29,250. Building 585,000; 585,000. Capital stock 390,000; 390,000. Cash 34,983; 66,660. Equipment (at cost) 13,260; 36,660. Land 89,700; 89,700. Merchandise inventory 29,835; 26,520. Note receivable, Diane Maynard 11,700; 0. Other noncurrent assets 4,857; 5,265. Other noncurrent liabilities 2,451; 2,451. Prepaid insurance 3,150; 2,826. Retained earnings 221,511; 229,446. Supplies on hand 5,559; 6,630. Taxes payable 5,700; 7,224.

A scanned textbook page: Cases, Case 3-1, Maynard Company (B), credited to Professor Robert N. Anthony; page footer 74 Part 1 Financial Accounting. Story in brief: Diane Maynard thanks her friend for the balance sheets from Case 2-1, Maynard Company (A), and asks why cash increased by $31,677 when net income was only $19,635. The friend says an income statement for June is a partial answer. Besides the (A) case data, the friend finds a record of cash receipts and disbursements (Exhibit 1), learns that all accounts payable were owed to vendors for merchandise inventory purchases, and that cost of sales in June was $39,345. Questions: 1. Prepare an income statement for June in proper format and explain how each item, including cost of sales, was derived. 2. Explain why the change in the cash balance was greater than net income. 3. Explain why (a) $14,715 and (b) $36,030 are incorrect cost of sales amounts for June, and under what circumstances they would be correct. Exhibit 1, Cash Receipts and Disbursements, Month of June. Cash receipts: Cash sales $44,420; Credit customers 21,798; Diane Maynard 11,700; Bank loan 20,865; Total receipts $98,783. Cash disbursements: Equipment purchased $23,400; Other assets purchased 408; Payments on accounts payable 8,517; Cash purchases of merchandise 14,715; Cash purchase of supplies 1,671; Dividends 11,700; Wages paid 5,660; Utilities paid 900; Miscellaneous payments 135; Total disbursements $67,106. Reconciliation: Cash balance, June 1 $34,983; plus Receipts 98,783; Subtotal $133,766; less Disbursements 67,106; Cash balance, June 30 $66,660.
